specimens.title: nerdhub
body: Study sites I built for my own courses. Each one turns a course's past papers into a place to read, practise and revise: notes, past questions, mock tests, flashcards, a mistakes list and a study plan.

Two sites live there now. PDSA Quiz 2 treats the course as a graph: every topic is marked visited, frontier or unvisited. The MLT platform reads like handwritten notes in pen-blue ink, with a formula drawer and search across every note and question.
facts: 5 topics · 159 past questions from 10 papers · course map, practice, mock exam, flashcards, last-night sheet
13 topics · 35 pages of Quiz 1 notes · practice next, mock test, cheatsheet, glossary, formula drawer
progress follows a student across devices, limited to IITM accounts by Firestore rules
specimens.fine: The study sites ask for an IITM student sign-in.
decisions: Adding a topic = add one data file and flip status to "ready". The engine never changes.
Built from the loaded topic data, so it never goes out of date.
The backend sits behind a small adapter (init, onAuth, signIn, signOut, load, save) so the logic can be tested without a network.
Firebase web config is public by design; who can read or write is decided by firestore.rules

specimens.title: This site
body: Drawn by hand in SVG, with no framework. Every fragment in the wings is redrawn from something worked out in nerdhub: a heap, a shortest-path graph, a recurrence, a decision tree, a regression fit, a nearest-neighbour sketch.
The geometry is computed by a small script and written out as plain HTML, so the page needs nothing to run. The motion is a layer on top; switch it off and the drawing is all still here.
related: where the fragments in the wings come from

specimens.title: Does adaptive practice help?
specimens.hook: a memory model, tested on 2,000 simulated students
body: MLT's “Practice next” ranks ideas by the marks you are likely to lose on them. Each idea carries a chance that you know it, updated after every answer (Bayesian knowledge tracing), and a memory half-life that doubles after a confident right answer and halves after a miss.

It was then tested against simpler ways of choosing. Most of the gain comes from weighting by marks: marks-weighted random gains 7.0 points over random, the full model 7.1. Over 30 days the memory model earns more (8.2 against 7.3). Practising your weakest topic first does worse than random.

The students are simulated, with a different forgetting law from the model, so it is tested on something it was not built for. It shows the method behaves sensibly. It does not show it helps real students.
Below are the recorded results for all five settings the simulation was run in. Nothing is re-simulated here.
facts: five: 7, 14 or 30 study days; 5, 10 or 20 questions a day; 49 ideas, marks from the real past papers
results from nerdhub/mlt/js/evidence.js; the simulation itself is not in this repository

specimens.title: A graph that lays itself out
specimens.hook: nodes push apart, edges pull together, then it cools
body: The PDSA site draws its graphs with its own force layout, about thirty lines long: every pair of nodes repels, every edge pulls its ends together, and each step is allowed to move a little less than the last, for 260 steps.

Below, the same code runs in your browser on real data: PDSA's five topics, joined to the topics each one builds on. Scrub through the 260 steps, play them, or pick a topic to see what it connects to.

specimens.title: A solver that shows where the work is
specimens.hook: type a recurrence; see which level of the tree pays
body: A small widget in PDSA's divide and conquer topic. You type a, b and d for T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(nᵈ) and it walks through the three steps of the master theorem, ending with why: the leaves do the most work, every level does the same, or the root does.
Below, choose a recurrence, or set a, b and d yourself, and read the work level by level down to the leaves.
related: the same rule, as one remember line

specimens.title: Remember lines
specimens.quote: Greedy = locally best, never undone. Fast, not always correct.
specimens.hook: one of 38 at the ends of PDSA's sections
body: Every section of the PDSA site ends in one line meant to survive the night before the exam. A few more:
lines: Height is cost. Balanced height is log n, a chain is n.
Heap = complete tree + parent-child order. Not sorted.
Relax: if dist[u]+w < dist[v], lower dist[v].
Compare a with bᵈ: bigger → n^(log_b a); equal → nᵈ log n; smaller → nᵈ.
specimens.lines_from: from nerdhub/pdsa-quiz-2/js/data/, maths typeset as plain text
related: that line, as a solver you can try

specimens.title: [FLAG]
specimens.hook: where the answer key was wrong, and the working
body: The MLT Quiz 1 notes tag every claim with where it came from, in the voice I wrote them in:
Across the 35 pages that comes to roughly 376 [SRC], 447 [ADDED] and 116 [FLAG] tags. Each [FLAG] is a place where the source or its answer key disagreed with the working, shown next to it.
specimens.legend: [SRC] = mere PYQ file se · [ADDED] = explanation / example / naya question · [FLAG] = source ya answer-key error, proof ke saath · [?] = unreadable / missing in source.
related: these notes are the MLT site's Quiz 1 pages

specimens.title: Two copies, one state
specimens.quote: Merge two copies of the study state without losing either.
specimens.hook: the rules at the top of merge.js
body: When the same student studies on two devices, both copies have to survive. The rules, as written in the file:
lines: past-question results: the newer attempt wins
counters: the larger count wins, because counters cannot be added without a log
a reset bumps the epoch, and a new epoch replaces instead of merging
specimens.lines_from: from the comment at the top of nerdhub/mlt/js/merge.js, lightly shortened
related: the answer log it merges is what Practice next reads
